title: Where does the third corner of this triangle go?
description: A base of four centimetres is drawn, then an arc of five centimetres from one end and an arc of six centimetres from the other. The crossing of the arcs is the third corner, and joining it to the ends gives the triangle. Keeko doubts the arcs and wants to draw a straight line of the right length.
teaching_notes: One idea: the third corner is the one place that is the right distance from both ends of the base, and two arcs find it. Watch for children who draw a straight line of the right length and hope its end lands in the right place.

source: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
video_script.why: The child has built a triangle with three equal sides and now builds one whose three sides are all different.
video_script.substitution: The base is four centimetres, the arc from one end has opening five centimetres and the arc from the other end has opening six centimetres.
video_script.anchor: A triangle with sides of four, five and six centimetres, drawn with a ruler and a compass
video_script.wrong_answer: a straight line of five centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: A child draws a straight line of the right length from one end and hopes its top end is in the right place, though a line can point in any direction.
video_script.payoff_line: Triangle eigh B C has sides of four, five and six centimetres.

final_answer.spoken: a triangle whose sides measure four, five and six centimetres

never_show: the finished triangle before the last step
maths_rules: arc from A with radius 5 cm: every place on it is 5 cm from A
arc from B with radius 6 cm: every place on it is 6 cm from B
C is on both arcs, so AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm
sides AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm
video_script.design: One idea: the third corner is the one place that is five centimetres from one end and six from the other. A base, two arcs in two colours, and the crossing; Keeko's doubt closes the video.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Build a triangle with sides of four, five and six centimetres.
<bookmark mark='find'/>How can we find the third corner once the base is drawn?

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a base of 4 cm with ends A and B; two dotted strips reach up from the ends toward an unnamed corner C

marks.five: a dotted strip of 5 cm reaches up from A
marks.six: a dotted strip of 6 cm reaches up from B

narration: <bookmark mark='base'/>Choose one of the lengths as the base, and we take four centimetres.
Call its ends eigh and B, and call the third corner C.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Then eigh C must be five centimetres.
<bookmark mark='six'/>And B C must be six centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Given: sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the three sides are four, five and six centimetres.

beats.on_screen: To find: the third corner C, and the triangle ABC
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to build the triangle by finding the third corner C.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: draw the base AB = 4 cm with the ruler

marks.base: the base AB of 4 cm is drawn

narration: <bookmark mark='base'/>Step one, draw the base eigh B, four centimetres long, with the ruler.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: compass point on A, opening 5 cm, long arc above the base

marks.arc_a: the arc from A is drawn above the base

narration: <bookmark mark='arc_a'/>Step two, put the compass point on eigh, open it to five centimetres, and draw a long arc.
<bookmark mark='reason'/>Every place on this arc is five centimetres from eigh.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: compass point on B, opening 6 cm, an arc that crosses the first arc

marks.arc_b: the arc from B is drawn and crosses the first arc

narration: <bookmark mark='arc_b'/>Step three, put the point on B and open the compass to six centimetres.
Draw an arc across the first arc.
<bookmark mark='reason'/>Every place on this arc is six centimetres from B.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: crossing = C; C is on both arcs, so AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm; join AC and BC

marks.join: AC and BC are drawn as straight sides

beats.colours: AC in blue, BC in orange
narration: <bookmark mark='cross'/>Step four, the crossing is C, and it lies on both arcs.
It is five centimetres from eigh and six centimetres from B.
<bookmark mark='join'/>Join C to both ends of the base.

beats.on_screen: Answer: triangle ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm

marks.ruler: a ruler lies along each side in turn

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Triangle eigh B C has sides of four, five and six centimetres.
<bookmark mark='ruler'/>A ruler check shows eigh B is four, eigh C is five and B C is six centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the finished triangle
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a straight line rises from the left end and swings to three different directions; then the arc from the right end marks the one place that fits

marks.doubt: a straight line rises from the left end of the base
marks.swing: the line swings to three different directions
marks.fix: the arc from the other end marks the one right place

beats.colours: the straight line in red, the arc in green
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we can draw a straight line of five centimetres up from the left end.
<bookmark mark='swing'/>A straight line can point in any direction, so its top end could be anywhere.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The arc from the other end finds the one place that is the right distance from both ends.
